title: The History Of The Israelites
segments: >> Dad,
can you tell us again where we come
from?
>> Yeah, the whole story from the
beginning.
>> All right, but this time pay close
attention because this isn't just
history, this is our story.
In the beginning, the Most High formed
Adam and Eve. He gave them laws, wisdom,
and dominion. From them began the family
of mankind.
But as wickedness spread, the Lord
flooded the earth
saving only one righteous man, Noah, and
his  family. Through the lineage
of Noah's son, Shem, came one of my
favorite forefathers,
Abraham,
a man of faith, obedience, and
righteousness.
A man who commanded  his
household according to the laws of the
Most High. Abraham had Isaac. Isaac had
Jacob and Esau, two manner of people
different from the womb.
Esau came out red all over like a hairy
garment, but Jacob, later named Israel,
chosen by the Most High to carry the
promise. Through Leah, Rachel, and his
two concubines,
>> Bilhah and Zilpah, Israel had 12 sons,
Reuben,
Simeon,
Levi,
Judah,
Issachar, Zebulun,
Dan,
Naphtali, Gad,
Asher,
Joseph,
>> and Benjamin.
When they were young,
Joseph
was hated by his brothers and sold
into slavery, carried into
Egypt. Through trials and faith, Joseph
rose from a  prisoner to second
in command over all Egypt. During this
time, he had two sons, Ephraim and
Manasseh.
When famine struck, his brothers came to
Egypt seeking help, not knowing the
powerful ruler before them was their own
brother.
Years later,
a new king in Egypt arose  which
knew not Joseph.
He enslaved our people with hard bondage
and oppression.
And the Most High raised up Moses
to deliver them. Pharaoh's heart
was hardened again and again.
So, the Lord plagued Egypt with mighty
signs and wonders.
Until finally, he parted the Red Sea and
let Israel through on dry ground.
And the Lord himself guided us, a pillar
of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by
night.
Moses ascended Mount Sinai, where the
Most High gave him the commandments,
which he delivered to our people,
laws to govern our nation.
But, because of disobedience,
our people wandered 40  years in
the wilderness,
until the Most High raised Joshua to
lead us into the promised land.
And during the era of the judges, the
Lord raised  up mighty men like
Gideon and Samson to deliver the
children of Israel from their enemies.
In our land,
Israel became a nation.
Saul was made our first king.
Then came David,
the young shepherd who slew Goliath and
ruled with righteousness. As king, David
reigned over Israel for 40 years, 7
years in Hebron and 33 years in
Jerusalem.
David's son Solomon ruled in unmatched
wisdom, but later,
>> he fell into sin. And because of that,
the kingdom split, northern kingdom and
southern kingdom.
The northern kingdom turned to idolatry
and was taken captive by the Assyrians.
Then Babylon invaded Judah,
destroying our temple and taking our
people into captivity.
>> After 70 years, leaders like Ezra and
Nehemiah returned to rebuild
Jerusalem and restore order.
During the reign of the Persian Empire,
our foremother Hadassah, whose name was
later changed to  Esther, was
raised up to become queen to King
Ahasuerus.
At that time, a wicked man named Haman
devised a deceitful plot to destroy all
the Israelites scattered throughout the
empire.
When Esther's cousin Mordecai learned of
the decree, he called upon Esther to
act. Risking her own life, went before
the king uninvited and revealed both her
identity and Haman's wicked
plot.
Haman was exposed and he was executed on
the very gallows he had prepared for
Mordecai.
In remembrance of this great reversal
and victory, Esther and Mordecai
established the two-day feast of Purim,
a memorial that our people
continue to keep to this day.
When the Greeks tried to erase our laws
and heritage, our forefathers, the
Maccabees, fought back and the temple
was rededicated. That's the feast of
dedication.
>> In time, Christ was born.
But Herod, fearing prophecy,
murdered the young children of Israel.
Christ taught the people, healed the
sick, cast  out devils, and
multitudes followed him. Christ taught,
healed, and moved the people.
And many believed on him, except the
scribes and Pharisees, who plotted
continually to destroy him. Christ was
betrayed, arrested,
and crucified.
He died for our sins, the sins of
Israel.
After his resurrection, the disciples
spread the gospel throughout our people.
Paul and the apostles traveled
throughout the lands
as the prophecies foretold,
teaching Israel scattered in Corinth,
Galatia, Rome, Ephesus, Philippi,
Thessalonica, and many other places.
>> [singing]
>> When Rome destroyed Jerusalem in 70 AD,
our people fled into  Africa,
Spain, and Portugal,
building great kingdoms across
both continents.
Centuries later,
in Spain and Portugal, the Inquisition
targeted us,  the Jews.
Then came the papal bulls,
laws permitting our capture and
enslavement.
From there began the transatlantic slave
trade.
Israelites shipped in chains to the
Americas, the Caribbean, and beyond.
We lost our names, heritage, language,
and laws,
just as the scriptures said we would.
But the Most High promised we would
remember ourselves.
Kimpa Vita, also known as Dona Beatriz,
taught in the early 1700s that Christ
and the Israelites were black. Gabriel
Prosser was born enslaved  in
Virginia around 1775.
Inspired by the Bible, he planned a
revolt in Richmond in 1800. Nat Turner,
known as the prophet,  was an
enslaved man in Virginia who led a
rebellion in 1831 after being moved by
Bible teachings and visions. William
Saunders Crowdy, 1896, established the
Church of God and Saints of Christ.
Although he taught blacks were God's
people, he mixed a lot of Christianity
in his teaching. Enoch Mgijima was a
force of prophet in South Africa who
formed a church called the Israelites in
the early 1900s. Frank S. Cherry
taught in the late 1800s that African
Americans were descendants of the
ancient Israelites. Wentworth A.
Matthews taught in the early 1900s that
African Americans were the original
Jews. Israel Ben Newman and Mordecai
Herman founded the Moorish Zionist
Temple in Harlem in 1921, one of the
earliest Hebrew Israelite congregations
in New York City.  Rabbi Arnold
Josiah Ford founded Beth B'nai Israel in
Harlem and became a spiritual influence
on Wentworth A. Matthews. The civil
rights movement rose  to national
prominence in the mid-1950s.
Leaders and groups like Martin Luther
King Jr., Malcolm X, fought against
segregation and racial discrimination
through the 1960s. Abba Bivens,
also known as Abba Bibbins,
>> taught in the mid-1900s that black
people, Latinos, and Native Americans
were all Israelites. Ben Carter, also
known as Ben Ammi, led about 300
Israelites from Chicago to Liberia in
the late 1960s
seeking to escape the curses and
oppression in America, but soon found
that hardship and political pressure
followed them overseas. Hulon Mitchell
Jr., also known as Yahweh  Ben
Yahweh, established the Nation of Yahweh
in the late 1970s. Mosheh Ben Kareem,
also known as Masha, helped carry on
Abba Bivens' teachings with Yaaqob in
the late 1960s and 1970s.
And in 1969, the truth rose again
through the works of the seven
elders.
And from that awakening from a small
